rationale: A wins because it keeps the story inside the supplied facts and turns every weak spot into a reporting requirement. Its best line, "A still-unprofitable public chain is betting the path to profit runs through automation," is a real tension. B has useful bones, but "$15 salad" and "premium fast-casual needs human hands" start decorating the pitch with facts the update did not give; that is how a decent angle walks itself into a correction.
gaps_in_A: "human-run ones" is a little loaded and less precise than the supplied fact, which says traditional stores, not necessarily fully human-run stores.
"Is there any current news peg here? None was supplied." overstates it. The expansion and newly shared margin data are a valid company-news peg; what is missing is an external newsjack peg.

The first two angles both lean on the same margin comparison. A distinguishes trade-unit economics from investor profitability well, but the founder would still need to choose one lead before pitching.
gaps_in_B: "The $15 salad" is invented. The update gives no price point, and cute specificity is still fake specificity.
"premium, customizable, ingredient-forward" and "the tier where automation couldn't go" are not in the update. That whole category thesis needs outside proof before it can carry an angle.
"The labor policy context — ongoing fights around restaurant-worker protections and minimum wage" adds a live backdrop the prompt did not provide. Fine if sourced later, not fine as grounding here.
"McDonald's, Chipotle's Autocado, etc." drags in competitors not supplied by the update and makes the third angle look more reported than it is.
